prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).

accepted: Non-convulsive status epilepticus following breakthrough generalized tonic-clonic seizure (subtherapeutic levetiracetam 8 µg/mL) with concurrent severe hepatic encephalopathy (ammonia 108) in alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 12); both lower consciousness to GCS 9.

differential.diagnosis: Severe hepatic encephalopathy (sole cause of GCS 9)
differential.key_features: Ammonia 108 + cirrhosis + asterixis = HE; but EEG is essential — cannot distinguish severe HE from NCSE clinically.
Post-ictal usually resolves within 30-60 minutes; persistence beyond raises NCSE concern.

differential.diagnosis: Anoxic brain injury from prolonged seizure
differential.key_features: MRI DWI if prolonged hypoxia; airway assessment.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Persistent unresponsiveness after a witnessed seizure mandates continuous EEG to exclude NCSE — clinical examination cannot distinguish severe HE from NCSE.
Cirrhotic patients on AEDs need adherence and level monitoring — subtherapeutic levels are a common breakthrough trigger.
Lacosamide and levetiracetam are AEDs of choice in cirrhosis (no significant hepatic adjustment).
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: EEG shows non-specific slowing and triphasic waves; the diagnosis is clinical with ammonia and precipitant identification.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F. is a 44-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis, prior seizure disorder treated with levetiracetam, and an established HE prophylaxis regimen, who was brought by ambulance in an unresponsive state. His girlfriend witnessed him having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure approximately 30 minutes before EMS arrival. He had been increasingly confused over the prior 2-3 days — she attributed it to usual HE episodes which he has had twice before. On the morning of presentation, he was more confused than usual, and then she found him on the floor seizing. He had been compliant with rifaximin and lactulose. He is 1 year sober. His levetiracetam had been recently increased from 500 mg BID to 1000 mg BID by his neurologist 3 weeks ago — girlfriend reports he may have missed some doses in the past week ('he kept forgetting'). On arrival he remains unresponsive with a GCS of 9.

neurological_exam.additional: GCS 9 — severely depressed consciousness after witnessed convulsive episode. Tongue laceration noted. Urinary incontinence during episode. Bilateral extensor plantar responses suggest post-ictal state or severe cerebral dysfunction. This could be: (1) prolonged postictal state from new seizure in known seizure disorder, (2) non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) after seizure, (3) severe HE (grade IV) presenting with GCS 9, or (4) any combination.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4 mm, equal, sluggishly reactive. Doll's eye reflex intact. No nystagmus.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 9 (E2V3M4). Minimally responsive. Does not follow commands. Eye opening to pain. Incomprehensible sounds. Purposeful withdrawal to pain. Asterixis cannot be assessed — GCS too low. Girlfriend reports he had a convulsive event 30 minutes before ambulance called.
neurological_exam.motor: Minimal spontaneous movement. Purposeful withdrawal pain.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses extensor (Babinski) bilaterally.
